title: 1 Kings 7:23–39
context: Hiram’s bronze work continues with the molten sea, a great round basin standing on twelve bronze oxen (7:23–26), and ten wheeled bronze bases, each carrying a bronze basin (7:27–39). 1 Kings does not state what these were used for, but the parallel at 2 Chronicles 4:6 says the basins were for washing the things that belonged to the burnt offering and that the sea was for the priests to wash in, in continuity with the bronze basin of the tabernacle (Exodus 30:18–21). Parallel differences, stated without harmonization: 1 Kings 7:24 describes buds under the brim of the sea, while 2 Chronicles 4:3 describes the likeness of oxen; 1 Kings 7:26 says the sea held two thousand baths, while 2 Chronicles 4:5 says it received and held three thousand. A bath is about one tenth of a cor, or about 5.6 U.S. gallons or 21 liters, so forty baths was about 224 gallons or 840 liters. “Sea” here can also be rendered pool or reservoir. Later history records that King Ahaz took the sea down from the oxen and removed the basins from the bases (2 Kings 16:17), and that the Chaldeans finally broke up the sea and the bases and carried the bronze to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13). Both traditions read this unit as constructive description, and neither assigns allegorical meanings to the oxen, wheels, or panels.

verses.text: He made the molten sea ten cubits from brim to brim, round in shape. Its height was five cubits; and a line of thirty cubits encircled it.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram makes the molten sea, ten cubits across, five high, thirty around. Arminian readers note the scale of the casting and the skill required. They read the measurements as practical description, given in round figures, and do not make them carry a theological or mathematical point the narrator does not raise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly treat the dimensions as historical description of a great bronze basin. They note that the account focuses on what was built for the LORD’s service rather than on precise engineering. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse plainly, and neither builds a doctrinal claim on the figures.

verses.text: Under its brim around there were buds which encircled it for ten cubits, encircling the sea. The buds were in two rows, cast when it was cast.
verses.arminianNotes: Buds encircle the sea under its brim in two rows, cast with it. Arminian readers see decorative craftsmanship integrated into the casting itself. The parallel at 2 Chronicles 4:3 describes oxen rather than buds, a difference recorded in the context without harmonization, and they see no need to resolve it by speculation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the buds as decoration and note the parallel difference honestly. They affirm that Scripture’s trustworthiness does not require every parallel detail to be harmonized on the page. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as craft description and decline to draw allegorical meaning from the ornament.

verses.text: It stood on twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, and three looking toward the west, and three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east; and the sea was set on them above, and all their hindquarters were inward.
verses.arminianNotes: The sea stands on twelve bronze oxen, three facing each direction. Arminian readers note the striking design and its symmetry. Many readers associate the number twelve with Israel’s tribes, but the text does not draw that connection, so they hold any such association loosely and do not make it a point of doctrine.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note that some interpreters link the twelve oxen to the twelve tribes, while recognizing that the text does not say so. Shared ground: both traditions treat the oxen as part of the sea’s construction and support, avoid building doctrine on proposed symbolism, and note that Ahaz later removed the sea from them (2 Kings 16:17).

verses.text: It was a hand width thick. Its brim was worked like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held two thousand baths.
verses.arminianNotes: The sea is a hand width thick, its brim like a lily, and it holds two thousand baths. Arminian readers note the elegance of the design and the great capacity. The parallel at 2 Chronicles 4:5 gives three thousand baths, recorded plainly in the context; the sea’s purpose is stated in 2 Chronicles 4:6 rather than here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same elegance and capacity and note that 2 Chronicles 4:6 says the sea was for the priests to wash in. Shared ground: both traditions connect the sea with priestly cleansing as the parallel describes, acknowledge the difference in capacity without forced harmony, and decline further allegory.

verses.text: He made the ten bases of bronze. The length of one base was four cubits, four cubits its width, and three cubits its height.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram makes ten bronze bases, each four cubits square and three high. Arminian readers note that the narrator gives careful attention to practical equipment for worship. These movable stands served the work of the house, and their detailed description honors the ordinary labor of service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the bases as practical furnishings for the LORD’s house, described with care. The detail reflects the ordered worship God provided for Israel. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as description of temple equipment and affirm that even practical items serve God’s worship.

verses.text: The work of the bases was like this: they had panels; and there were panels between the ledges;
verses.arminianNotes: The bases have panels set between ledges. Arminian readers see technical description of a skilled design. Like much of this section, the language is detailed and somewhat difficult to visualize, and they are content to receive it as a record of craftsmanship without seeking hidden meanings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also read the panels and ledges as construction detail. The narrator’s precision shows that the LORD’s house was built thoughtfully and well. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as straightforward description and agree that it raises no point of doctrinal difference.

verses.text: and on the panels that were between the ledges were lions, oxen, and cherubim; and on the ledges there was a pedestal above; and beneath the lions and oxen were wreaths of hanging work.
verses.arminianNotes: Lions, oxen, and cherubim decorate the panels, with wreaths beneath. Arminian readers note that cherubim appear throughout the temple and tabernacle decoration, associated with the holiness of God’s presence. The animals and wreaths add beauty without the text explaining their meaning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the recurring cherubim and the decorative lions and oxen, and they are cautious about assigning precise symbolism the narrator does not provide. Shared ground: both traditions read the decoration as fitting the holiness and beauty of the LORD’s house and decline to build doctrine on the images.

verses.text: Every base had four bronze wheels and axles of bronze; and its four feet had supports. The supports were cast beneath the basin, with wreaths at the side of each.
verses.arminianNotes: Each base has four bronze wheels with axles, and supports cast beneath the basin. Arminian readers note that the stands were mobile, practical equipment designed for real use. The verse shows careful engineering by Hiram in service of the house, with no doctrinal issue raised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same practical design and the care given to equipment used in worship. The account preserves the details of a real, working temple. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as technical description of movable stands and agree that it carries no separate theological dispute.

verses.text: Its opening within the capital and above was a cubit. Its opening was round like the work of a pedestal, a cubit and a half; and also on its opening were engravings, and their panels were square, not round.
verses.arminianNotes: The verse describes the round opening at the top of the base, with engravings and square panels. Arminian readers acknowledge that the technical terms are hard to picture today. They receive the detail as part of a faithful record of Hiram’s work and do not try to force a meaning from it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the difficulty of visualizing the opening and panels and treat the verse as craft description. Shared ground: both traditions are content to let technical details remain technical, affirming the trustworthiness of the record without speculating beyond what the text clearly states.

verses.text: The four wheels were underneath the panels; and the axles of the wheels were in the base. The height of a wheel was a cubit and half a cubit.
verses.arminianNotes: The wheels sit under the panels, with axles in the base, each a cubit and a half high. Arminian readers see further evidence of the careful design and construction of the stands. They read the measurements as practical specifications and do not make them a basis for doctrine.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly treat the wheels and axles as construction detail. The precision of the account honors the work of those who built the LORD’s house. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as straightforward description of the stands and agree that it raises no theological difference.

verses.text: The work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel. Their axles, their rims, their spokes, and their hubs were all of cast metal.
verses.arminianNotes: The wheels are like chariot wheels, with axles, rims, spokes, and hubs of cast metal. Arminian readers note the comparison to familiar chariot work, which helps the reader picture the stands. The narrator’s interest is in craftsmanship, and they decline to read symbolism into the wheels.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also read the chariot-wheel comparison as a practical description. They resist allegorizing the wheels, since the text presents them simply as part of the stands’ design. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as craft description and affirm the care taken in building equipment for worship.

verses.text: There were four supports at the four corners of each base. Its supports were of the base itself.
verses.arminianNotes: Four supports stand at the four corners of each base, part of the base itself. Arminian readers see a sturdy, integrated design suited to carrying heavy basins of water. The verse adds to the picture of skilled, purposeful work done for the LORD’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly read the supports as structural detail ensuring the stands would bear their load. The narrator records how things were made rather than what they might signify. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as straightforward description with no doctrinal disagreement in view.

verses.text: In the top of the base there was a round band half a cubit high; and on the top of the base its supports and its panels were the same.
verses.arminianNotes: A round band half a cubit high sits on top of each base, with its supports and panels. Arminian readers continue to read the description plainly. The cumulative detail shows how much care was invested in even the support equipment of the house, which they take as an example of diligent service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the cumulative detail as the narrator’s way of honoring the completeness and excellence of the work. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as construction description and affirm that no part of God’s house was treated as unimportant, without assigning symbolic meaning to the band.

verses.text: On the plates of its supports and on its panels, he engraved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, each in its space, with wreaths all around.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram engraves cherubim, lions, and palm trees on the plates and panels, with wreaths around. Arminian readers note that palm trees and cherubim also adorn the walls of the house (6:29), giving a unified design. The decoration expresses beauty in worship without the text explaining each figure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the continuity of cherubim and palm motifs between the stands and the house itself (6:29). They are cautious about precise symbolism the text does not give. Shared ground: both traditions read the engravings as fitting decoration for the LORD’s house and decline to allegorize them.

verses.text: He made the ten bases in this way: all of them had one casting, one measure, and one form.
verses.arminianNotes: All ten bases share one casting, one measure, and one form. Arminian readers note the consistency and quality control in Hiram’s work. Uniform equipment suited orderly worship, and the narrator’s summary emphasizes careful planning and execution rather than any hidden lesson.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same uniformity as reflecting the order appropriate to God’s worship. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a summary of the bases’ construction, affirming that ordered, careful work fits the orderly worship of the LORD’s house, while not making the casting itself a doctrine.

verses.text: He made ten basins of bronze. One basin contained forty baths. Every basin measured four cubits. One basin was on every one of the ten bases.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram makes ten bronze basins, each holding forty baths, one on each base. Arminian readers note that forty baths is often estimated at about 224 gallons. The large basins served practical cleansing needs in worship, as 2 Chronicles 4:6 explains, and the verse records their size plainly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the basins’ capacity and their washing function described in 2 Chronicles 4:6, in continuity with the tabernacle basin (Exodus 30:18). Shared ground: both traditions read the basins as serving the ritual cleansing God required in Israel’s worship and decline to allegorize them further.

verses.text: He set the bases, five on the right side of the house and five on the left side of the house. He set the sea on the right side of the house eastward and toward the south.
verses.arminianNotes: Hiram sets five bases on each side of the house and the sea on the right side of the house, toward the east and south. Arminian readers note the balanced arrangement that completes this section of the description. The placement served the work of the priests, and they read it as practical order for worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly read the arrangement as orderly placement of the furnishings. The same placement is recorded in 2 Chronicles 4:10. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the description of the sea and the stands, with no theological dispute raised by their positions.
